title: Large Scale Structure and Environmental Effects on Dwarf Galaxy Growth
summary: Dwarf galaxies serve as key models for understanding galaxy assembly in the early universe, with their final properties influenced by environmental factors. Using the dark matter-only simulation "Copernicus Complexio" (COCO) and the semi-analytic model GALFORM, we examine the stellar mass assembly of dwarf galaxies across different cosmic web regions, defined by the NEXUS+/CACTUS algorithm. We identify significant variations in stellar mass assembly based on final mass, with the largest dwarf galaxies assembling, on average, 50% of their mass 7.7 Gyrs later than the smallest ones. Central galaxies also differ in their assembly from satellites of comparable final mass, forming 50% of their mass 2.5 Gyrs later. The location within the cosmic web further influences assembly, with satellite galaxies showing greater differences than centrals. Satellites in the densest regions assemble their mass 1.5 Gyrs earlier than those in the least dense regions, compared to 0.69 Gyrs for central galaxies. This disparity arises from varying infall times, with satellites in dense environments infalling 5.2 Gyrs earlier than those in voids. Additionally, we investigate the impact of reionisation parameters, specifically the timing ($z_{cut}$) and filtering scale ($v_{cut}$) of reionisation. The stellar-to-halo-mass relation shows a power law break between $10^8~\mathrm{M}_\odot < M_{200} < 10^{10}~\mathrm{M}_\odot$, with earlier $z_{cut}$ or higher $v_{cut}$ leading to more star formation suppression in lower-mass haloes. The halo occupation fraction is also affected, with later $z_{cut}$ or lower $v_{cut}$ resulting in fewer lower-mass haloes being occupied at $z=0$. Our investigation provides a valuable theoretical framework for interpreting upcoming observational data in this mass regime.

AI.tldr: Dwarf galaxy assembly varies by mass, environment, and reionization parameters, with larger galaxies forming later, satellites assembling earlier in dense regions, and reionization timing affecting star formation suppression.
AI.motivation: To understand how dwarf galaxies assemble their stellar mass across different cosmic environments and how reionization parameters influence their formation, providing a theoretical framework for interpreting future observations.
AI.method: Used COCO dark matter-only simulation with GALFORM semi-analytic model, analyzed cosmic web regions via NEXUS+/CACTUS algorithm, and varied reionization parameters (z_cut timing and v_cut filtering scale).
AI.result: Largest dwarfs assemble 50% mass 7.7 Gyrs later than smallest; centrals form 2.5 Gyrs later than comparable satellites; satellites in dense regions assemble 1.5 Gyrs earlier than in voids; earlier z_cut/higher v_cut suppress star formation in low-mass haloes.
AI.conclusion: Dwarf galaxy assembly is strongly influenced by mass, environment (cosmic web location), and reionization history, with satellites showing greater environmental sensitivity than centrals, providing key insights for interpreting observational data.

title: Revealing the stellar population of the ultra-obscured Galactic globular cluster Glimpse-C02
comment: 9 pages, 8 figures. Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: In this paper, we present the results of a detailed photometric analysis of Glimpse-C02, one of the most extincted globular clusters of the Milky Way. We built a deep color magnitude diagram spanning $\approx$ 10 magnitudes, enabling the first identification of the cluster's main sequence turnoff. Due to the extreme reddening affecting the region, a differential reddening correction was necessary. The resulting reddening map reveals variations up to $δE(B-V) \approx 2.5$ mag. From isochrone-fitting of the differential reddening corrected color-magnitude diagram, we derived a mean color excess $E(B-V)=6.33^{+0.05}_{-0.04}$, and a distance modulus $(m-M)_0=14.00^{+0.26}_{-0.11}$, corresponding to a distance of $d=6.3^{+0.8}_{-0.3}$ kpc from the Sun, and a Galactocentric distance of $2.6^{+0.6}_{-0.7}$ kpc. This distance value, within the associated uncertainties, suggests that the cluster may be located closer to the Galactic Center compared to previous estimates, possibly supporting its classification as a bulge globular cluster. We obtained a photometric metallicity estimate of [Fe/H]$=-0.30^{+0.10}_{-0.08}$ and the first absolute age determination for Glimpse-C02, resulting in $t=11.9^{+0.7}_{-0.6}$ Gyr, as typically measured for Galactic globular clusters at this metallicity. We also derived a new estimate of the center of gravity of the cluster and determined its projected density profile from resolved star counts, finding a high King concentration parameter ($c = 1.97_{-0.67}^{+0.51}$) and a core radius $r_c =8.72^{+0.40}_{-0.35}$ arcsec. Finally, from the surface brightness profile of the system, we derived an integrated $H$-band magnitude $M_{\rm H}=-7.9$, corresponding to a mass of $M=3.57^{+0.22}_{-0.19}\times 10^4 M_{\odot}$. Thus, our work classifies Glimpse-C02 as an old and metal-rich globular cluster that is in an advanced stage of its dynamical evolution.

AI.tldr: Deep photometric analysis of heavily extincted globular cluster Glimpse-C02 reveals its first main sequence turnoff, extreme differential reddening, and refined distance placing it closer to Galactic Center as a bulge cluster.
AI.motivation: Glimpse-C02 is one of the most extincted globular clusters in the Milky Way, requiring detailed photometric analysis to overcome extreme reddening and determine its fundamental parameters for proper classification and understanding of its evolutionary state.
AI.method: Built deep color-magnitude diagram spanning ≈10 magnitudes, applied differential reddening correction to create reddening map, performed isochrone-fitting on corrected CMD, derived photometric metallicity and age, determined cluster center and projected density profile from star counts, analyzed surface brightness profile.
AI.result: First identification of main sequence turnoff; reddening variations up to δE(B-V)≈2.5 mag; mean color excess E(B-V)=6.33; distance d=6.3 kpc from Sun (2.6 kpc Galactocentric); photometric metallicity [Fe/H]=-0.30; age t=11.9 Gyr; high King concentration parameter c=1.97; core radius r_c=8.72 arcsec; integrated H-band magnitude M_H=-7.9; mass M=3.57×10^4 M⊙.
AI.conclusion: Glimpse-C02 is an old, metal-rich globular cluster in advanced dynamical evolution, likely located closer to Galactic Center than previously estimated, supporting classification as a bulge globular cluster.

title: The multi-age stellar populations of Terzan 5 as revealed by JWST
summary: The James Webb Space Telescope provides an exciting opportunity to investigate stellar systems located in heavily obscured regions like the Galactic bulge. Possibly, the most enigmatic among them is Terzan 5: long classified as a globular cluster, it is now known to host distinct stellar populations with different iron abundances (ranging approximately from [Fe/H]=-$0.8$ to [Fe/H]=$+0.3$ dex). Indeed the chemical and structural properties collected so far suggest that it is the remnant of one of the primordial clumps that contributed to the early assembly of the bulge, a so-called "Bulge Fossil Fragment". Here we present a new photometric analysis of Terzan 5 based on JWST/NIRCam observations in the F115W and F200W filters, as well as archival HST/ACS optical (F606W and F814W) data. The dataset overcomes the severe and spatially variable extinction along the line of sight and yields the deepest color-magnitude diagram ever obtained for Terzan 5. Proper motion selections and high-resolution differential reddening corrections allow us to isolate bona fide cluster members and to provide an unprecedented view of the main-sequence turn-off region. We clearly identify two main components and determine their respective ages: the old, sub-solar component has an age of 12.5 $\pm$ 0.5 Gyr, while the super-solar component is significantly younger with an age of 4.7 $\pm$ 0.5 Gyr. Interestingly, we also find hints of an even younger main sequence turn-off and sub-giant branch, consistent with the presence of a further stellar component with an age of 3.8 $\pm$ 0.5 Gyr. There is also evidence of a blue plume populated by stars as bright as $m_{\rm F115W}\sim 17.4$, suggesting a prolonged period of star formation extending up to 2.5 Gyr ago.

AI.tldr: JWST/NIRCam and HST/ACS observations of Terzan 5 reveal multiple stellar populations with distinct ages: 12.5 Gyr (sub-solar metallicity), 4.7 Gyr (super-solar), and 3.8 Gyr, plus evidence of star formation extending to ~2.5 Gyr ago, supporting its classification as a "Bulge Fossil Fragment."
AI.motivation: Terzan 5 is an enigmatic system in the Galactic bulge, originally classified as a globular cluster but now known to host distinct stellar populations with different iron abundances. Its chemical and structural properties suggest it may be a remnant of primordial clumps that contributed to the early assembly of the bulge, making it a potential "Bulge Fossil Fragment." The James Webb Space Telescope provides an opportunity to investigate such heavily obscured regions with unprecedented depth and clarity.
AI.method: Combined JWST/NIRCam observations in F115W and F200W filters with archival HST/ACS optical data (F606W and F814W). Applied proper motion selections and high-resolution differential reddening corrections to isolate bona fide cluster members. Analyzed color-magnitude diagrams to identify main-sequence turn-off regions and determine ages of different stellar components.
AI.result: Deepest color-magnitude diagram ever obtained for Terzan 5 reveals: 1) Old, sub-solar component with age 12.5 ± 0.5 Gyr, 2) Super-solar component with age 4.7 ± 0.5 Gyr, 3) Hints of even younger component with age 3.8 ± 0.5 Gyr, 4) Blue plume with stars as bright as m_F115W ~ 17.4, suggesting prolonged star formation extending up to 2.5 Gyr ago.
AI.conclusion: Terzan 5 contains multiple stellar populations with distinct ages spanning ~10 Gyr, supporting its classification as a "Bulge Fossil Fragment" - a remnant of primordial clumps that contributed to the early assembly of the Galactic bulge. The prolonged star formation history revealed by JWST observations provides crucial insights into the formation and evolution of the Galactic bulge.

title: Imladris: a detailed and flexible model for galaxy simulations with individual stars
summary: Coupling stellar feedback to the evolution of individual stars, as opposed to averaging over the initial mass function (IMF), substantially improves the fidelity of galaxy formation simulations by capturing stochastic population effects. Existing treatments can typically only operate at a narrow mass resolution range, limiting their applicability. We present Imladris, a detailed model for star formation and stellar feedback with individual stars. At high resolution, each star can be represented by its own particle ("star-by-star"). At coarser resolution, star particles represent specific realisations of stellar populations sampled from the IMF. Both methods share a unified implementation of stellar feedback tied to the individually tracked stars, including supernovae, stellar winds and radiation. Imladris has been optimised for both computational efficiency and memory footprint. We demonstrate the model with idealised galaxy simulations ($M_\mathrm{vir}\sim10^{10}-10^{11}\,\mathrm{M_\odot}$) spanning a baryonic mass resolution range of $2.5-1000\,\mathrm{M_\odot}$. Without re-calibration, the time-averaged star formation rate (SFR), galactic wind mass and energy loadings close to the disc are converged up to a resolution of $20\,\mathrm{M_\odot}$ within a factor of 1.1, 1.1 and 1.3, respectively, and 1.4, 1.6 and 2.5 up to $100\,\mathrm{M_\odot}$. Above this, SFRs become more bursty, while loading factors increase substantially. This is linked to resolution-dependent supernova clustering, which represents a fundamental barrier to convergence for any scheme attempting to model a self-consistent stellar feedback-regulated interstellar medium. Regardless, the ability to deploy the scheme across a wide range of resolutions (and to carry out in-depth resolution convergence studies) makes Imladris a powerful tool for numerical investigations of galaxy formation.

AI.tldr: Imladris is a star formation and feedback model that tracks individual stars across resolutions, showing convergence in key galaxy properties up to 100 solar mass resolution.
AI.motivation: Existing stellar feedback models are limited to narrow mass resolution ranges, restricting their applicability. There's a need for a model that can operate across wide resolution ranges while maintaining fidelity through individual star tracking.
AI.method: Imladris uses two approaches: at high resolution, each star is represented by its own particle ("star-by-star"); at coarser resolution, star particles represent specific realizations of stellar populations sampled from the IMF. Both share unified feedback implementation including supernovae, stellar winds, and radiation.
AI.result: The model demonstrates convergence in time-averaged star formation rates, galactic wind mass, and energy loadings up to 20 M⊙ resolution within factors of 1.1-1.3, and up to 100 M⊙ within factors of 1.4-2.5. Above 100 M⊙, SFRs become more bursty and loading factors increase substantially due to resolution-dependent supernova clustering.
AI.conclusion: Imladris enables deployment across wide resolution ranges and facilitates resolution convergence studies, making it a powerful tool for galaxy formation simulations despite fundamental convergence barriers related to supernova clustering.

title: Non-Cold Dark Matter from Memory-Burdened Primordial Black Holes
summary: Non-cold dark matter particles can arise from the evaporation of primordial black holes (PBHs). In this paper, we further investigate how the memory-burden effect, which delays the full evaporation of black holes, affects the Lyman-$α$ bound on such non-cold dark matter (NCDM) particles. We mainly focus on scenarios in which PBHs have fully evaporated by today, undergoing a semi-classical evaporation phase followed by a memory-burden dominated phase. In this framework, PBH evaporation generically leads to two distinct dark-matter populations with different velocity dispersions, which can imprint observable signatures on the matter power spectrum. We compute the resulting NCDM phase-space distribution and its impact on small-scale overdensities using the $\texttt{BlackHawk}$ and $\texttt{CLASS}$ codes. This is then used to reinterpret Lyman-$α$ forest constraints for thermal warm dark matter, deriving both a velocity-dispersion-based and a matter-power-spectrum-based estimate. In particular, we discuss how we obtain constraints on scenarios in which NCDM particles constitute only a fraction of the total relic dark matter. Finally, we discuss the viable parameter space as a function of dark matter masses, PBH initial conditions, and memory-burden parameters. We show that even subdominant NCDM components from PBH evaporation can be constrained, and confirm that NCDM can only account for all of the dark matter in the absence of PBH domination, as in the semi-classical case.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how the memory-burden effect in primordial black hole evaporation affects Lyman-α constraints on non-cold dark matter particles produced from PBH evaporation, showing that even subdominant NCDM components can be constrained.
AI.motivation: To understand how the memory-burden effect (which delays black hole evaporation) impacts constraints on non-cold dark matter particles produced from primordial black hole evaporation, particularly for Lyman-α forest observations.
AI.method: The authors study PBH evaporation scenarios where PBHs fully evaporate by today, with semi-classical evaporation followed by memory-burden dominated phases. They compute NCDM phase-space distributions using BlackHawk and CLASS codes, then reinterpret Lyman-α forest constraints for thermal warm dark matter using both velocity-dispersion-based and matter-power-spectrum-based estimates.
AI.result: PBH evaporation generically produces two distinct dark matter populations with different velocity dispersions that imprint observable signatures on the matter power spectrum. Even subdominant NCDM components from PBH evaporation can be constrained by Lyman-α observations. NCDM can only account for all dark matter in the absence of PBH domination, consistent with semi-classical cases.
AI.conclusion: The memory-burden effect significantly affects Lyman-α constraints on NCDM from PBH evaporation, allowing constraints on even subdominant dark matter components. The viable parameter space depends on dark matter masses, PBH initial conditions, and memory-burden parameters, with NCDM requiring absence of PBH domination to constitute all dark matter.

title: Lagrangian Bias as a Gaussian Random Field
summary: Halo bias is typically treated as a set of coefficients in a perturbative expansion. We show instead that every point in a Gaussian density field has a well-defined scale-independent Lagrangian bias, thereby defining a bias field. This property can be extended to any linear operator acting on the Lagrangian density field, generating secondary bias fields. Halo bias then arises from geometric selection of Lagrangian patches within this pre-existing field, rather than being generated by collapse. We demonstrate that this framework predicts the measured $b(M)$ relation for halos. The multivariate Gaussian structure of the fields naturally explains the Gaussian distribution of halo bias at fixed mass and assembly bias. The results presented here motivate combining this framework with a forward model of halo collapse, yielding an ab initio model for halo clustering.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a new framework where halo bias is treated as a pre-existing scale-independent field in Lagrangian space, rather than coefficients from perturbative expansion, explaining bias as geometric selection rather than collapse-generated.
AI.motivation: To move beyond the traditional perturbative treatment of halo bias as expansion coefficients and instead develop a more fundamental understanding of bias as an inherent property of the Gaussian density field.
AI.method: Define a scale-independent Lagrangian bias field for every point in a Gaussian density field, extend to linear operators generating secondary bias fields, and treat halo bias as geometric selection of Lagrangian patches within this pre-existing field.
AI.result: The framework successfully predicts the measured b(M) relation for halos and naturally explains the Gaussian distribution of halo bias at fixed mass and assembly bias through the multivariate Gaussian structure of the fields.
AI.conclusion: This approach provides a more fundamental basis for understanding halo bias and motivates combining it with forward models of halo collapse to create an ab initio model for halo clustering.

title: Eppur non si trovano Vol. 2: No Planetary-mass Primordial Black Holes toward the Andromeda Galaxy
comment: submitted to Acta Astronomica, comments on arXiv:2602.05840
summary: A recent preprint by Sugiyama et al. reported the discovery of twelve candidates for short-timescale (less than one day) gravitational microlensing events based on high-cadence photometric observations of the Andromeda Galaxy (M31) using the Subaru Hyper Suprime-Cam. These detections were attributed to a large population of planetary-mass primordial black holes (PBHs) that could account for the entirety of the dark matter in the Milky Way and M31 halos. However, these results are in clear tension with previous searches for short-timescale microlensing events toward the Magellanic Clouds, such as those by the OGLE survey. In addition, both the temporal and spatial distributions of the Subaru candidates are inconsistent with expectations for microlensing events. Here, we reanalyze the Subaru data using an independent difference image analysis photometric pipeline. We find that all twelve candidates identified by Sugiyama et al. exhibit asymmetric light curves and/or variability on multiple nights of Subaru observations. Our analysis reveals that among them ten objects are RR Lyrae stars, one is an eclipsing binary, and one is an unclassified variable star. We find no compelling evidence for short-timescale microlensing events among the candidates identified in the Subaru data set, nor for a significant population of planetary-mass PBHs as dark matter components. Our results underscore the necessity of robust variable-star rejection in high-cadence microlensing searches using large telescopes.

AI.tldr: Reanalysis of Subaru HSC data finds that 12 candidate short-timescale microlensing events are actually variable stars, not evidence for planetary-mass primordial black holes as dark matter.
AI.motivation: To critically examine Sugiyama et al.'s claim of detecting 12 short-timescale microlensing events in M31 that would support planetary-mass primordial black holes as dark matter, given inconsistencies with previous microlensing surveys and anomalous temporal/spatial distributions.
AI.method: Independent reanalysis of the same Subaru Hyper Suprime-Cam data using a different difference image analysis photometric pipeline, examining light curve characteristics and multi-night variability patterns.
AI.result: All 12 candidates show asymmetric light curves and/or multi-night variability; 10 are identified as RR Lyrae stars, 1 as an eclipsing binary, and 1 as an unclassified variable star. No evidence for genuine microlensing events or planetary-mass PBH population.
AI.conclusion: The claimed microlensing detections are misidentified variable stars, highlighting the critical importance of robust variable-star rejection in high-cadence microlensing searches with large telescopes.

title: The Star Formation Factory revisited I. The impact of metallicity on collapsing star-forming clouds
summary: Context. Stellar feedback regulates star formation and shapes the interstellar medium, yet its role during the collapse of molecular clouds remains uncertain over a wide range of initial conditions. Aims. We explore how stellar winds and supernovae influence star formation in collapsing gas clouds that span a broad parameter space in mass, size, and metallicity. Methods. Using a one-dimensional numerical model, we follow the evolution of feedback-driven bubbles produced by embedded clusters, incorporating time-dependent energy and mass injection, self-gravity, integrated cloud collapse, radiative cooling, shell instabilities, and triggered star formation. Our treatment of gas cooling in the hot bubble explicitly accounts for heat transfer across the bubble-shell interface. Results. We find that metallicity acts as a key regulator of feedback, comparable in importance to cloud mass and radius. In low-metallicity clouds, reduced radiative cooling is offset by weaker stellar winds, leading to prolonged star formation and higher efficiencies. Across a substantial portion of parameter space, the expanding shell undergoes a stalling phase that further enhances the star formation efficiency, an outcome that is not observed at higher metallicities. Conclusions. Our results suggest that the diverse properties of star clusters across cosmic time may arise from the metallicity-dependent interplay between stellar feedback and gas cooling.

AI.tldr: Metallicity regulates stellar feedback in collapsing molecular clouds, affecting star formation efficiency through cooling-wind balance and shell stalling.
AI.motivation: To understand how stellar feedback (winds and supernovae) influences star formation during molecular cloud collapse across diverse initial conditions, particularly the role of metallicity.
AI.method: One-dimensional numerical model tracking feedback-driven bubbles from embedded clusters, including time-dependent energy/mass injection, self-gravity, cloud collapse, radiative cooling, shell instabilities, and triggered star formation with explicit heat transfer across bubble-shell interface.
AI.result: Metallicity is as important as cloud mass/radius in regulating feedback. Low-metallicity clouds have reduced cooling offset by weaker winds, leading to prolonged star formation and higher efficiencies. Shell stalling phase enhances efficiency in substantial parameter space, not seen at higher metallicities.
AI.conclusion: Diverse star cluster properties across cosmic time may arise from metallicity-dependent interplay between stellar feedback and gas cooling.

title: Calibrating optical galaxy cluster projection effects with sparse spectroscopic samples: A clustering redshift approach
summary: Wide-field optical imaging surveys are efficient at identifying galaxy clusters, but optically identified clusters suffer from projection effects--physically unassociated galaxies along the line of sight can be misidentified as cluster members due to distance uncertainties. Previous studies have used spectroscopic follow-up observations of cluster members to quantify projection effects; however, such follow-up efforts cannot keep pace with the rapidly growing cluster samples. On the other hand, spectroscopic surveys designed for large-scale structure studies collect tens of millions of spectra but tend to have sparse spectra in cluster regions. To bridge this gap, we develop a clustering redshift approach that cross-correlates cluster members with sparse, non-cluster-targeted spectroscopic galaxy samples. We validate this approach using the Cardinal simulation, recovering the correct spectroscopic distribution and projection effect parameters of redMaPPer cluster members. Our approach is insensitive to the selection of the spectroscopic sample and paves the way for calibrating the upcoming LSST clusters using DESI and Roman spectroscopic samples.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a clustering redshift method to quantify projection effects in optically identified galaxy clusters by cross-correlating cluster members with sparse spectroscopic galaxy samples, validated using simulations.
AI.motivation: Optically identified galaxy clusters suffer from projection effects where unassociated galaxies along the line of sight are misidentified as cluster members due to distance uncertainties. Traditional spectroscopic follow-up cannot keep pace with rapidly growing cluster samples, while existing spectroscopic surveys have sparse coverage in cluster regions.
AI.method: Developed a clustering redshift approach that cross-correlates cluster members with sparse, non-cluster-targeted spectroscopic galaxy samples. Validated using the Cardinal simulation to recover the correct spectroscopic distribution and projection effect parameters of redMaPPer cluster members.
AI.result: The approach successfully recovers the correct spectroscopic distribution and projection effect parameters. The method is insensitive to the selection of the spectroscopic sample and enables calibration of upcoming LSST clusters using DESI and Roman spectroscopic samples.
AI.conclusion: The clustering redshift method provides an efficient way to quantify projection effects in optically identified clusters without requiring extensive spectroscopic follow-up, bridging the gap between optical cluster surveys and sparse spectroscopic data for large-scale structure studies.

title: Radiative Feedback in Population III Protostellar Growth: The Impact of HI Shielding
summary: We present a suite of radiation-magnetohydrodynamics simulations from the POPSICLE project that follow the long-term growth (~50 kyr) of primordial protostars while self-consistently coupling radiation, turbulence, and magnetic fields. The simulation suite is designed to quantify the relative impacts of the pathways of radiative feedback in Pop III stars - the extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) ionization and Lyman-Werner (LW) dissociation - by considering simulations with and without their inclusion. We find that without HI shielding, LW feedback alone can suppress and ultimately terminate accretion. With HI shielding, the large column densities near the protostar significantly weaken LW feedback. In the polar direction, atomic hydrogen fully shields LW radiation where $H_2$ self-shielding alone is insufficient. This leads to lower gas temperatures near the protostar and higher accretion rates, yielding larger final stellar masses than in models without shielding. The HII regions remain compact and confined to less than about 100 AU measured outward from the sink accretion radius (75 AU) due to high gas densities and continuous gas replenishment that inhibit the thermal pressure-driven breakout of the ionization front even for high ionizing luminosities. These results demonstrate that the interplay of gas dynamics, shielding, and radiative feedback can significantly alter the growth of Pop III stars. We discuss the implications for the initial mass function of primordial stars and the influence of feedback from early stellar populations.

AI.tldr: POPSICLE simulations show that Lyman-Werner feedback can suppress Pop III star accretion without HI shielding, but with HI shielding, accretion continues leading to larger stellar masses due to reduced gas temperatures near protostars.
AI.motivation: To quantify the relative impacts of different radiative feedback pathways (EUV ionization and LW dissociation) on primordial protostar growth, and understand how gas dynamics, shielding, and feedback interplay to alter Pop III star formation.
AI.method: Suite of radiation-magnetohydrodynamics simulations from POPSICLE project following ~50 kyr growth of primordial protostars with self-consistent coupling of radiation, turbulence, and magnetic fields; comparing simulations with and without EUV ionization and LW dissociation feedback.
AI.result: Without HI shielding, LW feedback alone suppresses and terminates accretion; with HI shielding, large column densities near protostar weaken LW feedback, atomic hydrogen fully shields LW radiation in polar direction leading to lower gas temperatures, higher accretion rates, and larger final stellar masses; HII regions remain compact (<100 AU) due to high gas densities and continuous replenishment inhibiting ionization front breakout.
AI.conclusion: Interplay of gas dynamics, shielding, and radiative feedback significantly alters Pop III star growth, with implications for primordial star initial mass function and feedback from early stellar populations.

title: Relic Magnetic Fields from Non-Adiabatic Photon Freeze-Out at Recombination
summary:
We propose a new mechanism for generating a primordial electromagnetic relic during the recombination--decoupling transition, based on the rate-dependent thermodynamics of the cosmic photon gas. Treating the photon sector as an open system coupled to the electron plasma, we show that a finite Thomson relaxation rate generates a departure from instantaneous thermal equilibrium, leading to non-adiabatic mode squeezing. As this relaxation rate rapidly decreases across recombination, the system quickly loses the ability to further amplify the deviation, and the squeezing freezes out at a small but finite value. This dynamics is naturally described as a narrow transition layer between an adiabatic tracking regime and a post-relaxation freeze-out regime. By a canonical transformation, the reduced evolution equation is recast into a forced oscillator with a smooth effective potential, clarifying the origin of the squeezing and the selection of the relic scale.
  Projecting the resulting non-equilibrium electromagnetic relic onto the magnetic sector, we derive the corresponding spectrum and show that its characteristic peak is controlled not by the squeezing parameter alone but by the weighted combination \(k^3\mathscr S_k\). In representative realizations, the peak corresponds today to scales of order \(10\)--\(20\) Mpc, while the present-day field amplitude remains extremely small. The mechanism is therefore better viewed as a source of a frozen non-equilibrium electromagnetic relic than as a complete explanation of the observed cosmic magnetic fields.

AI.tldr: A new mechanism generates primordial electromagnetic relics during recombination via Thomson relaxation rate-dependent thermodynamics, creating non-adiabatic mode squeezing that freezes out as a small-scale electromagnetic relic.
AI.motivation: To explain the origin of primordial electromagnetic fields in the early universe by identifying a new mechanism that operates during the recombination-decoupling transition, addressing the longstanding puzzle of cosmic magnetic field origins.
AI.method: Treat the photon sector as an open system coupled to electron plasma, analyze rate-dependent thermodynamics with finite Thomson relaxation rate, derive non-adiabatic mode squeezing dynamics, and recast evolution via canonical transformation into forced oscillator with smooth effective potential.
AI.result: The mechanism produces a frozen non-equilibrium electromagnetic relic with characteristic peak scales of 10-20 Mpc today, where the spectrum peak is controlled by weighted combination k³S_k rather than squeezing parameter alone, yielding extremely small present-day field amplitudes.
AI.conclusion: The proposed mechanism generates a primordial electromagnetic relic during recombination via Thomson relaxation dynamics, but produces field amplitudes too small to fully explain observed cosmic magnetic fields, serving better as a source of frozen non-equilibrium electromagnetic relics than a complete explanation.

title: A Comprehensive Analysis of WISE Mid-Infrared Colors for Obscured AGN Selection
summary: In this paper, we investigate the robustness of WISE mid-IR color selection (W1-W2) for identifying obscured (Type 2) active galactic nuclei (AGNs) at low redshift (z<0.3), using a sample of ~360,000 SDSS galaxies classified via emission lines into Seyfert 2 (Sy2), LINER, and star-forming (BPT-SF) galaxies. We find that the K-correction is essential to remove non-AGN contamination, and once applied the simple W1-W2>0.5 selection emerges as optimal in terms of purity and completeness of AGN selection. However, we confirm that even this lenient cut selects only ~13% of Sy2 galaxies and that achieving W1-W2>0.5 requires AGN contributing >75% of the total infrared luminosity, which is uncommon. Although mid-IR-selected Sy2s tend to be luminous, the high [OIII] luminosity does not guarantee red W1-W2 (nor does any other tested global or NLR-scale parameter), suggesting the critical role of obscuration on smaller scales. <1% of BPT-SF systems (but making ~20% of all mid-IR selected galaxies) exhibit W1-W2>0.5 colors. Such colors cannot be reproduced by models of star-heated dust alone. Red BPT-SFs tend to have higher W4 luminosities than expected from SF, indicating true AGNs. Intriguingly, mid-IR AGNs in massive bulges ($M_{\mathrm{bulge}} \gtrsim 10^{10} M_{\odot}$) predominantly (84%) manifest themselves as BPT-AGNs, whereas those in low-mass bulges ($\lesssim 10^{10} M_{\odot}$) mostly (60%) manifest as BPT-SF. This BPT-AGN vs.\ BPT-SF dichotomy does not extend to total stellar mass. We conclude that although the mid-IR AGN selection is incomplete, its strength lies in identifying optically inconspicuous AGNs with low-mass bulges, regardless of the total mass.

AI.tldr: WISE mid-IR color selection (W1-W2>0.5) effectively identifies obscured AGNs at low redshift but is incomplete (only ~13% of Sy2 galaxies), requiring AGN to dominate IR luminosity (>75%). The method reveals optically inconspicuous AGNs in low-mass bulges.
AI.motivation: To evaluate the robustness and limitations of WISE mid-infrared color selection (W1-W2) for identifying obscured (Type 2) AGNs at low redshift, particularly assessing its completeness, contamination, and dependence on host galaxy properties.
AI.method: Analyzed ~360,000 SDSS galaxies at z<0.3 classified via emission lines (BPT diagram) into Seyfert 2, LINER, and star-forming galaxies. Applied K-correction to WISE mid-IR colors, tested W1-W2 selection criteria, and examined correlations with AGN luminosity fractions, host bulge masses, and other parameters.
AI.result: W1-W2>0.5 emerges as optimal selection after K-correction, but selects only ~13% of Sy2 galaxies. Achieving this color requires AGN to contribute >75% of total IR luminosity. Mid-IR-selected Sy2s are luminous but high [OIII] luminosity doesn't guarantee red W1-W2. <1% of BPT-SF systems show W1-W2>0.5 (20% of all mid-IR selected galaxies). Mid-IR AGNs in massive bulges (≥10¹⁰ M☉) mostly (84%) appear as BPT-AGNs, while those in low-mass bulges mostly (60%) appear as BPT-SF.
AI.conclusion: Mid-IR AGN selection is incomplete but valuable for identifying optically inconspicuous AGNs, especially in low-mass bulges. The W1-W2>0.5 criterion effectively selects obscured AGNs after K-correction, though requiring strong AGN dominance in IR luminosity. The BPT-AGN vs. BPT-SF dichotomy depends on bulge mass rather than total stellar mass.

title: A Geometric Theory of Cosmological Structure via Entropic Curvature in Wasserstein Space
summary: We construct a geometric framework for cosmological large-scale structure based on optimal transport theory and Wasserstein geometry. In this framework, Ricci curvature on the probability measure space $\mathcal{P}_2(M)$ is characterized by the geodesic convexity of entropy and is formulated as the response of probability distributions to optimal transport. We introduce effective Ricci curvatures $K_{\mathrm{eff}}^{(\infty)}$ and $K_{\mathrm{eff}}^{(N)}$ associated with Kullback--Leibler-type and Rényi-type entropies, corresponding respectively to the curvature-dimension conditions CD$(K,\infty)$ and CD$(K,N)$. By localizing these curvatures to finite scales using local and reference measures, we construct curvature indicators applicable to observational data. Under a local quadratic approximation, the effective curvature reduces to the Hessian of the log-density, showing that conventional Hessian-based structure classifications arise as a limiting case of the present framework. We further show that effective curvature depends on observational scale and formulate this dependence as a scale flow, distinct from Ricci flow because it describes a change of resolution rather than a time evolution of geometry. Treating curvature as a random field then extends the statistical description of density fields: curvature statistics are given by higher-order weighted integrals of the power spectrum and by spatial derivatives of the correlation function, emphasizing geometric rather than amplitude information. This framework provides a unified connection between optimal transport geometry and cosmological structure analysis, and offers a new perspective on multiscale structure and nonlinear statistics.

AI.tldr: A geometric framework for cosmological large-scale structure analysis using optimal transport theory and Wasserstein geometry, introducing effective Ricci curvatures that connect to conventional Hessian-based methods and provide multiscale structure characterization.
AI.motivation: To develop a more fundamental geometric framework for analyzing cosmological large-scale structure that goes beyond conventional density field statistics, connecting optimal transport theory with cosmological structure analysis and providing new tools for multiscale geometric characterization.
AI.method: Constructs a geometric framework based on optimal transport theory and Wasserstein geometry on probability measure spaces. Introduces effective Ricci curvatures K_eff^(∞) and K_eff^(N) associated with Kullback-Leibler and Rényi entropies, corresponding to curvature-dimension conditions CD(K,∞) and CD(K,N). Localizes curvatures to finite scales using local and reference measures, applies local quadratic approximations, and formulates scale dependence as a scale flow distinct from Ricci flow.
AI.result: Shows that conventional Hessian-based structure classifications arise as a limiting case of the framework when using local quadratic approximations. Demonstrates that effective curvature depends on observational scale and can be treated as a random field, with curvature statistics given by higher-order weighted integrals of the power spectrum and spatial derivatives of correlation functions, emphasizing geometric rather than amplitude information.
AI.conclusion: Provides a unified connection between optimal transport geometry and cosmological structure analysis, offering a new perspective on multiscale structure and nonlinear statistics that emphasizes geometric information over conventional amplitude-based approaches.

title: X-ray variability of SDSS J000532.84+200717.4: from a normal state to an X-weak state
summary: We present a multi-epoch study of the extreme X-ray variability of the type~1 quasar SDSS~J000532.84+200717.4 using archival observations from \textit{XMM-Newton}, \textit{Swift}/XRT, \textit{EP-FXT}, and \textit{ROSAT}, together with new optical spectroscopy and multi-wavelength photometry. The 0.2--10~keV X-ray flux exhibits a transition from a high state to a subsequent low state, declining by more than an order of magnitude and placing the source in the X-ray--weak regime ($Δα_{\rm ox} \lesssim -0.3$). Significant variability on timescales of days to weeks persists within the low state. In contrast, the optical and mid-infrared emission remain stable over decade-long timescales, while the UV continuum varies only mildly and broadly tracks the X-ray evolution. Multi-epoch optical spectroscopy shows no significant long-term changes in either the continuum shape or the broad emission-line profiles. The \ion{Mg}{2} emission is relatively weak compared with typical quasars, suggesting similarities to weak-line quasars. The pronounced wavelength-dependent variability indicates that the accretion disk remains largely intact while the X-ray emission undergoes dramatic changes. The spectral hardening in the low state and the viability of ionized partial-covering models are consistent with variable, largely dust-free absorbing gas, possibly associated with clumpy inner disk winds, although intrinsic coronal variations cannot be excluded. SDSS~J0005+200717.4 therefore provides evidence that extreme X-ray weakness can arise as a transient phase in otherwise normal quasars.

AI.tldr: Multi-epoch study reveals extreme X-ray variability in quasar SDSS J0005+200717.4, transitioning from high to low state with >10× flux decline while optical/IR remain stable, suggesting transient X-ray weakness in normal quasars.
AI.motivation: To investigate extreme X-ray variability in type 1 quasar SDSS J0005+200717.4 and understand the physical mechanisms behind dramatic X-ray flux changes while optical/IR emission remains stable.
AI.method: Multi-epoch analysis using archival X-ray observations (XMM-Newton, Swift/XRT, EP-FXT, ROSAT) combined with new optical spectroscopy and multi-wavelength photometry to study variability across timescales from days to decades.
AI.result: X-ray flux declined by >10× from high to low state, placing source in X-ray-weak regime; optical/mid-IR stable over decades; UV mildly tracks X-ray; Mg II emission weak suggesting weak-line quasar characteristics; spectral hardening in low state.
AI.conclusion: Extreme X-ray weakness can be a transient phase in otherwise normal quasars, likely caused by variable absorbing gas (possibly clumpy inner disk winds) rather than intrinsic coronal changes, while accretion disk remains intact.

title: Euclid preparation. Impact of redshift distribution uncertainties on the joint analysis of photometric galaxy clustering and weak gravitational lensing
summary: One of the $\textit{Euclid}$ mission's key projects is the so-called 3$\times$2pt analysis, that is, the combination of cosmic shear, photometric galaxy clustering, and galaxy-galaxy lensing. Although $\textit{Euclid}$ has established quality requirements for the photo-$z$ accuracy needed for the weak lensing galaxy sample, no such requirements have been set for the photometric clustering sample. In this paper, we investigate the impact of redshift uncertainties on $\textit{Euclid}$'s photometric galaxy clustering analysis and its combination with weak gravitational lensing, focusing on data release 1 (DR1). In particular, we study whether having precise knowledge of the mean of the redshift distributions per bin is sufficient to avoid biases in the resulting cosmological constraints or whether accuracy in the higher-order moments of the distribution is required. We evaluate the results based on their constraining power on $w_{\mathrm{0}}$ and $w_{a}$ and define thresholds for the precision and accuracy of $\textit{Euclid}$'s redshift distribution of the photometric clustering sample. We find that the redshift distributions of the photometric clustering sample must be known at an accuracy of 0.004(1+$z$) in the mean in order to recover 80$\%$ of the constraining power in $\textit{Euclid}$'s DR1 $w_{\mathrm{0}}w_{a}$CDM 3$\times$2pt analysis. The impact of the uncertainty on the width is negligible, provided the mean redshift is constrained with sufficient accuracy. For most sources of redshift distribution error, attaining the requirement on the mean will also reduce uncertainty in the width well below the required level.

AI.tldr: Euclid's photometric galaxy clustering analysis requires redshift distribution accuracy of 0.004(1+z) in the mean to recover 80% of constraining power for dark energy parameters, with width uncertainty being negligible if mean is sufficiently constrained.
AI.motivation: Euclid mission lacks quality requirements for photometric clustering sample redshift accuracy, unlike weak lensing sample. Need to determine impact of redshift uncertainties on 3×2pt analysis (cosmic shear + galaxy clustering + galaxy-galaxy lensing) and establish accuracy thresholds for DR1.
AI.method: Investigate impact of redshift uncertainties on Euclid's photometric galaxy clustering analysis and combination with weak lensing. Study whether precise knowledge of mean redshift distributions per bin is sufficient or higher-order moments are required. Evaluate based on constraining power on w₀ and wₐ dark energy parameters.
AI.result: Redshift distributions must be known at accuracy of 0.004(1+z) in the mean to recover 80% of constraining power in Euclid's DR1 w₀wₐCDM 3×2pt analysis. Width uncertainty is negligible if mean is sufficiently constrained. For most error sources, achieving mean requirement reduces width uncertainty below required level.
AI.conclusion: Euclid's photometric clustering sample requires precise mean redshift knowledge (0.004(1+z) accuracy) for unbiased cosmological constraints, with width uncertainty being secondary. This establishes clear quality requirements for DR1 analysis.

title: Revisiting Marked Galaxy Clustering from a Joint Point Process Perspective
summary: Marked correlation functions, in which galaxy properties such as luminosity or stellar mass are treated as marks, are widely used to test models of galaxy formation. In astronomy, however, these statistics are typically implemented as summary measures that do not preserve the joint structure of mark pairs conditioned on separation. In this work, we formulate galaxies as points $(x,m)$ on the product space $\mathbb{R}^3\times\mathcal{M}$, where $x$ denotes position and $m$ a mark, and introduce the joint pair correlation function $g(r;m_1,m_2)$ as the fundamental quantity describing mark-dependent clustering. We further define a diagnostic quantity $Δ_{\mathrm{ind}}(r;m_1,m_2)$ that locally quantifies deviations from the independence hypothesis relative to spatial clustering alone, thereby providing a projection-free description of which mark pairs are over- or underrepresented at a given separation scale. Within this framework, commonly used diagnostics such as the inhomogeneous cross-$J$ function are naturally interpreted as summary statistics obtained through averaging over mark sets and geometric-event-based reductions of the joint structure. This perspective clarifies that previously discussed marked effects, including assembly bias, correspond to projections of an underlying joint dependence, and that observationally accessible information is the existence of non-factorizable joint structure itself. The present formulation provides both a fundamental quantity and practical diagnostics for its characterization.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the joint pair correlation function as a fundamental quantity for analyzing mark-dependent galaxy clustering, providing a projection-free diagnostic for deviations from independence between marks at different separation scales.
AI.motivation: Current marked correlation functions in astronomy are typically implemented as summary measures that lose the joint structure of mark pairs conditioned on separation, limiting detailed analysis of mark-dependent clustering patterns.
AI.method: Formulate galaxies as points (x,m) on product space ℝ³×ℳ, define joint pair correlation function g(r;m₁,m₂) as fundamental quantity, and introduce diagnostic Δ_ind(r;m₁,m₂) to quantify deviations from independence hypothesis relative to spatial clustering alone.
AI.result: Provides a framework where commonly used diagnostics like inhomogeneous cross-J function are interpreted as summary statistics obtained through averaging over mark sets, clarifying that previously discussed marked effects correspond to projections of underlying joint dependence.
AI.conclusion: The formulation offers both a fundamental quantity and practical diagnostics for characterizing mark-dependent clustering, preserving joint structure information that is lost in traditional summary measures.

title: Transport-Geometric Formulation of Peak Statistics: Curvature-Conditioned Point Processes and Response Hierarchy
summary: We develop a geometric formulation of peak statistics in cosmological density fields based on optimal transport and entropy. In this framework, the density field is treated as a probability measure, and its local structure is characterized by the Hessian of the log-density, which arises as the local response of an entropy functional in Wasserstein space. Peaks are thereby defined as positive-curvature stationary points, and their number density is expressed as a curvature-conditioned point process. In the linear Gaussian limit, the joint distribution of local variables closes in terms of a finite set of spectral moments, recovering the standard theory of peak statistics, known as BBKS. This clarifies that BBKS corresponds to a solvable limit of a more general structure combining probability distributions, curvature constraints, and geometric measure. The framework extends naturally beyond Gaussianity and linearity. Deviations from Gaussianity are incorporated as deformations of the joint distribution of curvature variables, while nonlinear structures are described through the curvature of the log-density. We further derive the two- and three-point peak statistics as curvature-conditioned $n$-point measures, and show that the full hierarchy of peak statistics can be organized as response functions to long-wavelength background modes. In this formulation, the conventional peak bias appears as the lowest-order response coefficient, with higher-order correlations arising as its natural extensions. This work embeds peak theory into a unified geometric framework and provides a systematic basis for incorporating nonlinearity, non-Gaussianity, and higher-order statistics, with direct relevance for observational applications.

AI.tldr: A geometric formulation of cosmological peak statistics using optimal transport and entropy, treating density fields as probability measures and characterizing peaks via Hessian of log-density, extending beyond Gaussian/linear limits.
AI.motivation: To develop a unified geometric framework for peak statistics that extends beyond the limitations of standard BBKS theory, incorporating nonlinearity, non-Gaussianity, and higher-order statistics in a systematic way.
AI.method: Uses optimal transport and entropy theory to treat density fields as probability measures, defines peaks as positive-curvature stationary points via Hessian of log-density, expresses statistics as curvature-conditioned point processes, and organizes hierarchy as response functions to background modes.
AI.result: Recovers BBKS in Gaussian limit, derives two- and three-point peak statistics, shows peak bias emerges as lowest-order response coefficient with higher-order correlations as natural extensions, and provides systematic framework for nonlinear/non-Gaussian extensions.
AI.conclusion: Embeds peak theory into unified geometric framework that systematically incorporates nonlinearity, non-Gaussianity, and higher-order statistics, providing foundation for observational applications beyond traditional Gaussian/linear limitations.

title: OJALÁ: Optimizing J-PAS Astronomy for Large-scale Analysis. A foundation model for the SED of galaxies, QSOs and stars
summary: The advent of large-scale surveys requires efficient ML techniques to exploit the information of massive datasets. We present OJALA, a transformer-based autoregressive foundation model designed to simultaneously classify astronomical objects and infer their physical parameters using 54 narrow bands from J-PAS, combined with broad bands from the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys and WISE. The model is trained on $\sim20$ million synthetic SEDs generated from DESI DR1 spectra. We validate OJALA using a cross-matched sample of $\sim121,000$ objects between J-PAS and DESI. The model achieves a weighted F1-score of approximately 0.9 for spectral classification (stars, galaxies, and QSOs) at $i < 21$. For galaxies, we recover photo-z with a precision of $σ_{\rm NMAD} < 0.01$, while for QSOs, the precision improves significantly at $z > 1.5$, reaching $σ_{\rm NMAD} \approx 0.006$ at $z \approx 3.5$. We demonstrate robust estimation of physical properties for galaxies, recovering stellar masses and SFR with a scatter of approximately 0.11 dex and 0.22 dex, respectively. Furthermore, the model accurately predicts EWs for major optical emission lines, allowing for the derivation of extinction-corrected H$α$ luminosities with a scatter of 0.29 dex. OJALA successfully reproduces the BPT and WHAN diagnostic diagrams, classifying SF, AGN, and passive galaxies with F1-scores typically ranging from 70% to 90% depending on the diagnostic class. For stars, the model reliably infers effective temperature and metallicity, though surface gravity remains challenging. Finally, we show the modularity of the architecture by fine-tuning the pre-trained embeddings to predict BH masses, a property not included in the primary training, recovering spectroscopic virial estimates with a precision of approximately 0.5 dex. We release the code, model weights, and a comprehensive VAC for the J-PAS EDR.

AI.tldr: OJALA is a transformer-based foundation model for astronomical object classification and physical parameter inference using multi-band photometric data from J-PAS and other surveys, achieving high accuracy across various tasks.
AI.motivation: Large-scale astronomical surveys generate massive datasets requiring efficient ML techniques to extract information. There's a need for models that can simultaneously classify objects and infer physical parameters from photometric data.
AI.method: OJALA uses a transformer-based autoregressive architecture trained on ~20 million synthetic SEDs generated from DESI DR1 spectra. It processes 54 narrow bands from J-PAS combined with broad bands from DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys and WISE.
AI.result: Achieves weighted F1-score ~0.9 for spectral classification (stars, galaxies, QSOs) at i<21. For galaxies: photo-z precision σ_NMAD<0.01; for QSOs: σ_NMAD≈0.006 at z≈3.5. Recovers stellar masses (0.11 dex scatter), SFR (0.22 dex), Hα luminosities (0.29 dex). Classifies SF, AGN, passive galaxies with F1-scores 70-90%. Infers stellar Teff and metallicity. Modular architecture allows fine-tuning for BH mass prediction (0.5 dex precision).
AI.conclusion: OJALA demonstrates state-of-the-art performance for simultaneous classification and physical parameter inference from photometric data. The model's modularity enables extension to new properties. The release of code, weights, and VAC facilitates community use for J-PAS EDR analysis.

title: Universal Non-Gaussian Signatures from Transient Instabilities
summary: We identify universal signatures in the bispectrum arising from a transient tachyonic instability of entropic fluctuations during inflation, a phenomenon that naturally arises in hyperbolic field-space geometries. We perform exact numerical calculations directly at the level of fluctuations, without relying on a specific background model, and distinguish two cases. In the light case, with masses around the Hubble scale, our results provide the first-ever computation of the bispectrum due to such tachyonic instabilities. We find a universal magnification of the folded configuration, together with the known non-analytic scaling in the squeezed limit. As an illustrative example, we compute and analyse the bispectrum in angular inflation, demonstrating compatibility with current limits. In the heavy case, with masses well above the Hubble scale, the bispectrum exhibits a distinctive correlation between enhanced folded configurations and a `tachyonic resonance' in mildly squeezed limits, with the resonance scale set by the strength of the instability. While the main qualitative features are reproduced, we show that there exists no UV matching for which a single-field effective description, obtained by integrating out the entropic modes, accurately captures the bispectrum for all kinematic configurations. To facilitate observational applications, we introduce simple bispectrum shape templates suitable for current and forthcoming cosmological surveys. Our model-independent results allow for constraining non-standard inflationary attractors characterised by strongly non-geodesic motion.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies universal bispectrum signatures from transient tachyonic instabilities of entropic fluctuations during inflation in hyperbolic field-space geometries, distinguishing light and heavy mass cases and providing templates for observational constraints.
AI.motivation: To understand and characterize universal signatures in the bispectrum arising from transient tachyonic instabilities of entropic fluctuations during inflation, which naturally occur in hyperbolic field-space geometries, and to develop observational constraints for non-standard inflationary attractors with strongly non-geodesic motion.
AI.method: Perform exact numerical calculations directly at the level of fluctuations without relying on specific background models, distinguish light (masses around Hubble scale) and heavy (masses well above Hubble scale) cases, compute bispectrum in angular inflation as illustrative example, and introduce simple bispectrum shape templates for observational applications.
AI.result: For light masses: first-ever computation of bispectrum from tachyonic instabilities showing universal magnification of folded configuration and non-analytic scaling in squeezed limit. For heavy masses: distinctive correlation between enhanced folded configurations and 'tachyonic resonance' in mildly squeezed limits with resonance scale set by instability strength. No single-field effective description accurately captures bispectrum for all kinematic configurations.
AI.conclusion: Universal bispectrum signatures from transient tachyonic instabilities provide observational probes for non-standard inflationary attractors with strongly non-geodesic motion; simple templates facilitate constraints from current and future cosmological surveys, while single-field effective descriptions fail to fully capture the bispectrum features.

title: Predicting CO and dust emission of star-forming galaxies
comment: 15 pages, accepted for publication in A&A
summary: How do Dwarf Galaxies differ from spirals? Does star formation produce radio and far-infrared emission in the same way as in spiral galaxies? Radio, FarIR, and CO emission depend on gas density, temperature, magnetic field strength, and metallicity. The radio-FarIR correlation and Schmidt-Kennicutt relation characterize the links for Milky Way-like galaxies but do they hold for smaller objects, with different morphologies? Here we extend our previous work on the IR, line, and radio emission of local and high-z galaxies to local star-forming low-mass and dwarf galaxies. The calculation of the cosmic ray (CR) densities were improved compared to the previous version of the model. The CR ionization rate we found for the different galaxy samples is higher by a factor of three than for the solar neighborhood. This means that the mean yield of low-energy CR particles three times higher in external galaxies than was observed by Voyager I. The dependence of the N_H2/I_CO factor on the metallicity and stellar mass are calculated by the model. The weaker CO emission from low-metallicity galaxies is due to the large amount of (CO-dark) H_2 surrounding the regions where CO is not photo-dissociated. Within our model framework, star-forming low-mass and dwarf galaxies follow the radio-IR correlation.

AI.tldr: This paper extends galaxy emission modeling to low-mass and dwarf galaxies, finding they follow the radio-IR correlation despite different CR densities and CO-dark H₂ fractions.
AI.motivation: To determine if established relationships between radio, far-infrared, and CO emission that hold for Milky Way-like spiral galaxies also apply to low-mass and dwarf galaxies with different physical properties (gas density, temperature, magnetic fields, metallicity).
AI.method: Extended previous galaxy emission modeling framework to local star-forming low-mass and dwarf galaxies, with improved cosmic ray density calculations and modeling of the N_H2/I_CO factor dependence on metallicity and stellar mass.
AI.result: Found cosmic ray ionization rates 3× higher than solar neighborhood, indicating more low-energy CR particles in external galaxies. Weaker CO emission in low-metallicity galaxies explained by large CO-dark H₂ reservoirs. Star-forming low-mass and dwarf galaxies follow the radio-IR correlation.
AI.conclusion: Despite different physical conditions (higher CR densities, metallicity-dependent CO-dark H₂), the fundamental radio-IR correlation holds for dwarf galaxies, suggesting star formation produces radio and far-infrared emission similarly across galaxy types.

title: Curvature-induced electroweak symmetry breaking and phase transition of a Higgs-portal dark scalar field
comment: 16 pages, 6 figures, based on the talk in the "Workshop on Standard Model and Beyond 2025" (24 Aug - 3 Sep 2025) of the Corfu Summer Institute 2025 "School and Workshops on Elementary Particle Physics and Gravity" (CORFU2025)
summary: This overview of the study arXiv:2407.18845, regarding the possibility of generating gravitational waves from a curvature-induced phase transition of a non-minimally coupled scalar dark matter field with a Higgs-portal, was showcased at the "Workshop on Standard Model and Beyond 2025" of the Corfu Summer Institute 2025. The phase transition dynamics during the transition from inflation to kination were calculated for various inflationary scales, considering both positive and negative values of the non-minimal coupling, while also examining the potential for triggering electroweak symmetry breaking. Notably, kination enhances the GW amplitudes, significantly restricting the viable parameter space. While the GW spectra follow the usual rule for high-frequencies from high inflationary scales, certain regions of the parameter space allow for a potential detection with future experiments.

AI.tldr: Study examines gravitational wave generation from curvature-induced phase transitions of non-minimally coupled scalar dark matter with Higgs-portal during inflation-to-kination transition, finding kination enhances GW amplitudes and restricts parameter space.
AI.motivation: Investigate gravitational wave production from phase transitions in non-minimally coupled scalar dark matter models during cosmological transitions, particularly exploring connections between dark matter, Higgs physics, and gravitational wave signatures.
AI.method: Calculate phase transition dynamics during inflation-to-kination transition for various inflationary scales, considering both positive and negative non-minimal coupling values, and examine potential for triggering electroweak symmetry breaking.
AI.result: Kination enhances gravitational wave amplitudes, significantly restricting viable parameter space. While high-frequency GW spectra follow usual patterns from high inflationary scales, certain parameter regions allow potential detection with future experiments.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that curvature-induced phase transitions in non-minimally coupled scalar dark matter models can produce detectable gravitational wave signals, with kination playing a crucial role in amplifying amplitudes and constraining model parameters.

title: Cosmological zoom-in perturbation theory as a consistent beyond point-particle approximation framework
summary: Modelling structure formation across the full dynamical range of the Universe remains a major challenge in cosmology. This difficulty originates from a fundamental limitation of geodesics in general relativity: a one-parameter family of geodesics can cease to be geodesic at a finite time. This implies that the conventional point-particle approximation is not the primary issue; rather, the breakdown of geodesic flow restricts a consistent description across scales. We develop a covariant multi-scale framework that resolves this problem by decomposing spacetime into hierarchical regions separated by matter horizons. We show how to match shared boundary consistently at the level of the action, leading to a covariant backreaction contribution. The resulting construction provides a first-principles theoretical foundation for cosmological zoom-in simulations and yields an effective energy-momentum tensor capturing the impact of the geometric backreaction effect. As an application, we demonstrate that this backreaction naturally produces flat galaxy rotation curves without invoking an additional dark matter component. Our results establish a new perspective on nonlinear structure formation, in which long dynamical range is resolved through a hierarchy of discrete geodesic domains.

AI.tldr: A covariant multi-scale framework resolves geodesic flow breakdown in cosmology by decomposing spacetime into hierarchical regions separated by matter horizons, providing theoretical foundation for zoom-in simulations and explaining flat galaxy rotation curves without dark matter.
AI.motivation: The fundamental limitation in cosmology is that geodesics in general relativity can cease to be geodesic at finite times, preventing consistent description of structure formation across scales. The conventional point-particle approximation is not the primary issue; rather, the breakdown of geodesic flow restricts multi-scale modeling.
AI.method: Develop a covariant multi-scale framework that decomposes spacetime into hierarchical regions separated by matter horizons. Match shared boundaries consistently at the action level, leading to covariant backreaction contributions. This yields an effective energy-momentum tensor capturing geometric backreaction effects.
AI.result: The construction provides a first-principles theoretical foundation for cosmological zoom-in simulations. The framework's backreaction naturally produces flat galaxy rotation curves without invoking additional dark matter components, demonstrating its physical relevance.
AI.conclusion: Establishes a new perspective on nonlinear structure formation where long dynamical range is resolved through a hierarchy of discrete geodesic domains, overcoming fundamental limitations of geodesic flow in general relativity.

title: Distance and [Fe/H] of Galactic bulge clusters from member RR Lyrae I-band light curves
comment: 8 pages, 3 Figures, 2 Tables. The data used in this work are available in the OGLE IV database. The results in the form of tables can be shared on request to the corresponding
summary: We have investigated the results for [Fe/H] and distance for a group of 24 globular clusters in the Galactic bulge, employing recent calibrations of RR Lyrae light curves Fourier decomposition and period-absolute magnitude-metallicity (PMZ) calibrations in the I-band. We have limited our calculations to RR Lyrae stars that have been proven to be very likely cluster members. These results are compared with [Fe/H] and Mv (distance) obtained from well-established Fourier calibrations in the V-band. These calibrations of the I-band were found to produce iron values that can differ from the UVES spectroscopic scale by -0.29 to +0.15 dex. The PMZ distances agree within 0.4 kpc with recent solid critical distance compilations. Adopting the newly derived distances, we conducted a spatial and orbital analysis of the bulge globular clusters in a non-axisymmetric Milky Way potential, and compared their orbital properties with earlier studies, finding broadly consistent trends with small systematic differences driven by the assumed distances and Galactic model. Clusters associated with the in situ bulge component display a narrow range low angular momentum and low orbital energies, consistent with formation in the early inner Milky Way.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates metallicities and distances of 24 Galactic bulge globular clusters using I-band RR Lyrae Fourier decomposition and PMZ calibrations, compares results with V-band methods, and analyzes cluster spatial/orbital properties in a non-axisymmetric Galactic potential.
AI.motivation: To derive improved metallicity and distance estimates for bulge globular clusters using updated I-band RR Lyrae calibrations, and to understand their spatial distribution and orbital characteristics within a realistic non-axisymmetric Galactic potential.
AI.method: Used I-band RR Lyrae light curve Fourier decomposition and period-absolute magnitude-metallicity (PMZ) calibrations for 24 bulge globular clusters, limited to confirmed cluster members. Compared results with established V-band Fourier calibrations. Conducted spatial and orbital analysis in a non-axisymmetric Milky Way potential using newly derived distances.
AI.result: I-band iron values differ from UVES spectroscopic scale by -0.29 to +0.15 dex. PMZ distances agree within 0.4 kpc with recent critical distance compilations. In situ bulge clusters show narrow range of low angular momentum and low orbital energies, consistent with early inner Milky Way formation.
AI.conclusion: The I-band RR Lyrae calibrations provide reliable metallicity and distance estimates for bulge globular clusters. Orbital analysis reveals distinct properties for in situ bulge clusters, supporting their formation in the early inner Galaxy. The methodology offers improved constraints for understanding bulge cluster populations and their formation history.

title: ALMA Band 2 line survey of a $z = 3.44$ clumpy strongly-lensed submillimetre galaxy
comment: 8 pages; 5 figures, submitted to MNRAS. Comments warmly welcomed
summary: I present the first molecular line survey of the strongly lensed submillimetre galaxy SPT 0027 ($z = 3.44$) using the new Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) Band~2 receivers (67 - 116 GHz), whose commissioning completes ALMA's full (sub-)millimetre frequency coverage. The broad spectral coverage from 76 to 111 GHz of the observations simultaneously accesses a large suite of molecular and atomic emission lines. I report the novel detections of the hitherto inaccessible CO (3-2) and HNC (4-3) lines, as well as detections of previously-observed CO (4-3) transitions, the neutral carbon line [CI], HCN (5-4), HCO$^{+}$ (5-4), and HNC (5-4), with fluxes in line with previous observations. The CO spectral line energy distribution and [CI]/CO line ratios indicate highly excited, dense molecular gas with a strong far-ultraviolet radiation field. The dense gas fraction is estimated at $17 \pm 9$ per cent, consistent with other dusty star-forming galaxies selected from wide-area surveys. High-resolution Band 7 continuum imaging reveals a clumpy lensed morphology, with star-forming clumps contributing 30-50 per cent of the total emission. With multiple CO lines accessible across a wide redshift range, ALMA Band 2 is uniquely positioned as the premier tool for robust spectroscopic redshifts at Cosmic Noon and beyond ($z \sim 1$-$6$), a capability that will be further enhanced by the Wideband Sensitivity Upgrade's full-band coverage in fewer tunings.

AI.tldr: First molecular line survey of lensed galaxy SPT 0027 using ALMA Band 2 reveals novel CO (3-2) and HNC (4-3) detections, showing highly excited dense gas with strong UV radiation field and clumpy star formation.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate the capabilities of newly commissioned ALMA Band 2 receivers (67-116 GHz) for molecular line surveys of high-redshift galaxies, particularly for accessing previously inaccessible transitions and enabling robust spectroscopic redshift determination at Cosmic Noon (z~1-6).
AI.method: Used ALMA Band 2 receivers for broad spectral coverage (76-111 GHz) to conduct molecular line survey of strongly lensed submillimeter galaxy SPT 0027 at z=3.44, combining with high-resolution Band 7 continuum imaging.
AI.result: Novel detections of CO (3-2) and HNC (4-3) lines, plus detections of CO (4-3), [CI], HCN (5-4), HCO+ (5-4), and HNC (5-4). Analysis shows highly excited, dense molecular gas with strong far-UV radiation field, dense gas fraction of 17±9%, and clumpy lensed morphology with star-forming clumps contributing 30-50% of total emission.
AI.conclusion: ALMA Band 2 is uniquely positioned as the premier tool for robust spectroscopic redshifts at Cosmic Noon and beyond (z~1-6), with capabilities that will be further enhanced by the Wideband Sensitivity Upgrade's full-band coverage.

title: The radial component of the local Galactic magnetic field in 3D
comment: 18 pages, 14 figures, accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: We present a distance-resolved reconstruction of the local line-of-sight Galactic magnetic field, $B_{||}$, by combining a 3D electron density map, $n_e$, derived from dust-map-informed simulations, with a full-sky map of Faraday rotation measure (RM). Our forward model evaluates RM on the same 3D grid as the $n_e$ map and compares it to the Galactic Faraday rotation sky. We infer $B_{||}$ using a Gaussian-process prior whose power spectrum is inferred from the data with geometric variational inference. The result is a local map of $B_{||}$, with uncertainties, within 1.25 kpc for $b>5$ deg. The reconstructed RM sky reproduces prominent features of the Faraday rotation sky, with a root-mean-square average field strength of $1.63 \pm 0.16$ $μ$G. In face-on views, the magnetic field shows coherent patches with alternating sign and hints of kpc-scale modulations, together with significant structure on scales of order 100 pc. The reconstructed $B_{||}$ field has a 3D power spectrum with an average slope of $-2.73 \pm 0.19$. We validate the $B_{||}$ reconstruction using Galactic pulsars. Predicted RMs, computed by integrating $n_e B_{||}$ to each pulsar distance, correlate with observed RMs. Predicted dispersion measures from the $n_e$ map also correlate with measured DMs, although with significant scatter.

AI.tldr: A 3D reconstruction of the local Galactic magnetic field's line-of-sight component (B_∥) within 1.25 kpc using dust-informed electron density maps and Faraday rotation measurements.
AI.motivation: To create a distance-resolved map of the local Galactic magnetic field by combining 3D electron density information with Faraday rotation measurements, enabling detailed study of magnetic field structure in the Milky Way.
AI.method: Forward modeling approach combining 3D electron density maps from dust-informed simulations with full-sky Faraday rotation measurements. Uses Gaussian-process prior with inferred power spectrum and geometric variational inference to reconstruct B_∥ on a 3D grid.
AI.result: Reconstructed B_∥ map within 1.25 kpc showing coherent patches with alternating sign, kpc-scale modulations, and 100 pc-scale structure. Average field strength of 1.63±0.16 μG, power spectrum slope of -2.73±0.19. Validation with pulsars shows correlation between predicted and observed RMs and DMs.
AI.conclusion: Successfully reconstructed distance-resolved local Galactic magnetic field using combined electron density and Faraday rotation data, revealing complex magnetic structure with validation from pulsar measurements.

title: First results of AMBRA: Abundant Seeds and Early Mergers as a Pathway to the First Massive Black Holes
comment: 22 pages, 13 figures, submitted to ApJ. Comments are welcome!
summary: AMBRA combines the large cosmological volume and statistical power of ASTRID with the physically motivated gas-based black hole seeding models from BRAHMA. Motivated by JWST's discoveries of massive black holes (BHs) at $z\gtrsim 9$, AMBRA adopts a lenient heavy-seed prescription from the BRAHMA suite, allowing for the formation of $4\times 10^{4-5}\ M_{\odot}$ seeds in halos with star-forming, metal-poor gas. The seeding model is motivated by scenarios in which heavy seeds form through stellar collisions in star clusters or from the rapid growth of Population III remnants. The improved seeding model enables AMBRA to form BH seeds much earlier and more efficiently compared to ASTRID. This significantly enhances early BH growth, producing a $z=8$ BH number density more than an order of magnitude higher than that in ASTRID over the mass range $10^{5-7}\ M_{\odot}$. BHs reaching masses consistent with GN-z11 and CEERS-1019 typically originate in highly compact density peaks and undergo multiple early mergers. In these systems, $\sim50\%$ of BH masses by $z=11$ is from BH mergers, after which gas accretion becomes the dominant growth channel. Without this early merger-driven assembly, ASTRID cannot reproduce the high-mass BH detected by JWST. Our results indicate that abundant early seed formation combined with frequent mergers can explain several JWST massive BH candidates without requiring sustained super-Eddington accretion. As a testable prediction, AMBRA yields $\approx4$ LISA detectable BH merger events per year at $z\geq8$, which is three orders of magnitude higher than that in ASTRID.

AI.tldr: AMBRA combines ASTRID's cosmological volume with BRAHMA's gas-based BH seeding, enabling early formation of massive BH seeds that explain JWST observations through mergers rather than sustained super-Eddington accretion.
AI.motivation: Motivated by JWST's discoveries of massive black holes at z≳9, the paper aims to explain how such early massive BHs could form, addressing the limitations of previous simulations like ASTRID which couldn't reproduce these observations.
AI.method: AMBRA combines the large cosmological volume and statistical power of ASTRID with BRAHMA's physically motivated gas-based black hole seeding models. It adopts a lenient heavy-seed prescription allowing formation of 4×10⁴⁻⁵ M⊙ seeds in halos with star-forming, metal-poor gas, motivated by stellar collisions in clusters or rapid growth of Population III remnants.
AI.result: AMBRA forms BH seeds earlier and more efficiently than ASTRID, producing z=8 BH number density >10× higher over 10⁵⁻⁷ M⊙ range. BHs matching GN-z11 and CEERS-1019 masses originate in compact density peaks and undergo multiple early mergers, with ~50% of BH mass by z=11 from mergers. Without early merger-driven assembly, ASTRID cannot reproduce JWST detections. AMBRA predicts ≈4 LISA-detectable BH merger events per year at z≥8, three orders of magnitude higher than ASTRID.
AI.conclusion: Abundant early seed formation combined with frequent mergers can explain several JWST massive BH candidates without requiring sustained super-Eddington accretion. The enhanced merger rate provides testable predictions for gravitational wave observatories like LISA.
